evidence_quotes.quote: In 2016, 94.6% of Panama’s population had access to drinking-water through pipework, and 74.6% received potable drinking-water, more likely within the urban area. There are no records of drinking-water quality supplied by the 5,619 aqueducts from the countryside, because the legal regulation (Reglamento Técnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99) has not been applied for these type of aqueducts.
In both countries, the rectory is week and fractioned. As a result, national drinking-water policies have been proposed that seek to achieve universal access for the year 2030.

Por tal motivo se presenta el siguiente documento, cuyo objetivo general consiste en “realizar un análisis comparativo sobre el acceso a los servicios de agua potable entre Panamá y Costa Rica, además de su relación con los indicadores de salud pública y desarrollo, con el propósito de identificar las fortalezas y debilidades que permitan definir metas a mediano y largo plazo”.

Por otro lado, la experiencia como Director del Laboratorio Nacional de Aguas (LNA) y la preparación de informes anuales de cobertura y calidad del agua [14, 15], permiten definir la situación actual del acceso a agua potable en Costa Rica.
El Reglamento Técnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 [20], sobre la calidad del agua potable, no abarca los acueductos rurales.
En el cuadro 4 se observan los totales regionales de viviendas ocupadas y ocupantes, con y sin agua, según la Encuesta Nacional de Hogares de Costa Rica de julio del 2016 [21].

criterion_notes.c1: Examines national, urban, and rural access to piped drinking-water supply and potable water coverage in Panama and Costa Rica, including dwelling connection categories in Costa Rica.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and a rigorous plain reading of Criterion 2 as an access determinant. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the paper does not examine any rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory rules governing connection or exclusion). Instead, the legal instruments discussed (Panama's Reglamento Tecnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 and Decreto Ejecutivo 353; Costa Rica's Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S and PNMSCSAP Decreto Ejecutivo 33953-S-MINAET) concern potable water-quality monitoring and potability standards in existing aqueducts (rural Panama aqueducts already supply piped water to 20% of the population, and non-application of DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 only leaves rural water quality unrecorded), while references to weak fragmented stewardship (rectoria) and 2030 national policy proposals (PNAPS) are unanalysed macro-governance background and policy recommendations. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, although the text mentions regulatory agencies (ASEP, DISAPAS, ARESEP), water-quality decrees, public/municipal/community operator shares, and sector stewardship, none of these is empirically analysed as an exposure governing service access (Cuadro 2 compares potability within already-served populations, and the comparative analysis treats water coverage as an explanatory factor for public-health indicators), so plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Compiles descriptive quantitative secondary data from national utility/regulator inventories and water-quality surveillance (ASEP, DISAPAS, 2010 Census, LNA), Costa Rica's July 2016 National Household Survey (ENAHO), and PAHO/WHO health and socioeconomic statistics, although structured as a descriptive situational diagnosis rather than an analytical study design.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports population coverage of piped drinking water (94.6% in Panama; 97.6% in Costa Rica), occupied dwellings and occupants with indoor pipe, exterior pipe, or no pipe in Costa Rica (Cuadro 4), provincial and indigenous comarca unserved rates in Panama, and potable water coverage.
criterion_notes.c5: Populations and descriptive water-coverage outcomes are identifiable, and the study is a descriptive cross-national situational comparison, but there is no identifiable empirical exposure-outcome design testing a legal, administrative, or governance exposure on service access; instead, national water coverage is descriptively juxtaposed with public-health and development indicators and 2030 SDG targets.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English title and abstract. Although Spanish is not exempt under Criterion 9 (English, Portuguese, Dutch), direct comprehension/translation from the provided Spanish full text by the AI screener is feasible per Criterion 10, allowing full substantive assessment.

study_design: Descriptive cross-national comparative situational study using secondary administrative, water-surveillance, census, and household survey data
country: Panama and Costa Rica (with Central American comparison tables for health and socioeconomic indicators)
population_and_sample: National urban and rural populations of Panama (estimated 4,058,372 inhabitants; 130 urban and 5,619 rural aqueducts) and Costa Rica (4,889,762 inhabitants across 1,465,259 occupied dwellings and 2,588 aqueducts in 2016), plus 7 Central American countries in secondary health/socioeconomic tables
exposure: Cross-national comparison of national drinking-water coverage between Panama and Costa Rica (treated as a correlate of public health and development indicators), with descriptive references to potable water-quality regulations (DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99, Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S, PNMSCSAP), operator shares, and proposed 2030 national policies; no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing service access is analysed
outcome: Population and dwelling piped drinking-water coverage (indoor pipe, exterior pipe, no pipe) and potable-quality water coverage, alongside national public health and socioeconomic indicators (life expectancy, under-5 mortality, communicable disease rate, literacy, GDP per capita, health expenditure)
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure). This Spanish-language full-text article presents a descriptive two-country situational diagnosis comparing aggregate piped drinking-water coverage and water potability in Panama and Costa Rica, relating national coverage to macro public-health and development indicators across Central America, and outlining 2022/2030 SDG policy targets. It does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Its legal and regulatory references (such as Panama's Reglamento Tecnico DGNTI-COPANIT 23-395-99 not covering rural aqueducts and Costa Rica's Decreto Ejecutivo 38924-S and PNMSCSAP) concern drinking-water quality monitoring and potability classification rather than rules governing service access or connection, while discussions of fragmented sector stewardship (rectoria) and proposed national policies (PNAPS 2017-2030) are unanalysed macro-governance background and policy recommendations.
